doc.title: Bill Mays interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 5, 2025

title: Joy and listening in current jazz
summary: Asked about joy in today's jazz, he wants players to listen, communicate and be agenda-less.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: No, no. I love tangents. I’m wondering if you think joy has become something that the current generation of jazz musicians – how do I phrase this – seems less important than gravitas. I just got a letter from a former student who witnessed a jazz trio in a club in San Francisco I guess, and he just described it as if it was they were fighting to get something out to the audi – actually that they just were playing for themselves and it was like a competition, an athletic competition or something. I’m not verbalizing my question very well, but joy does not seem to be as much a part of jazz as it used to be.

Yeah well I’m thinking, over the last six months of groups that I’ve heard where it was joyful, where they were locked in, where it was effortless and they were communicating to me. And then I’m remembering groups where it’s more like what you just described, where they sound like they’re trying to impress me with how fast they can play or how many notes they can play. I guess what I really want to hear in other groups when I go to listen and what I want to give when I play is a sense that we’re listening to one another, communicating, we’re playing off of each other, we’re making a group musical painting, and we’re playing the musical situation. You know I’m going to play differently on a real

slow ballad like “Lush Life” than I’m going to play when I’m playing a walking ballad like “Darn that Dream.” And I’m going to play a little differently if I’m playing it solo than if I’m playing with a trio. I think the key here, I’m getting off into the weeds I don’t really know where I’m going at this moment. I think what’s important is – and this sounds kind of corny – but to try to be as agenda-less as possible. To try to let the music chart the direction. Listen to one another, let the music take it where it wants to go. Don’t try to force the issue, try to be as agenda-less as possible.
You know Bill, I quoted a couple of musicians earlier in this interview and I believe I’ll be quoting you in some of my future ones.
